2.summary: A network-based intrusion detection system (NIDS) is required for monitoring activity on multiple systems; it analyzes all traffic that travels across the network.
2.deeper: A NIDS can be its own network device or software on a system. It looks for suspicious activity, logs the details and sends out an administrative alert. Its components work together. A sensor, software or hardware placed on each network segment, collects that segment's traffic and forwards it to the analysis engine, or to a collector if the infrastructure has one; the collector gathers traffic from the sensors and sends it on. The analysis engine analyzes the packets to determine whether they are suspicious. The console is where alerts and notifications are typically sent, and where the administrator configures the NIDS.
2.analogy: A NIDS is like a building's camera system: cameras in each hallway, a recorder that gathers the feeds, someone who studies them, and a control desk where the alarms ring.
2.scenario: An Airman sets up a NIDS for a network with two segments. A sensor on each segment collects its traffic and forwards it to a collector, which sends it to the analysis engine. When the engine finds suspicious packets, an alert arrives at the console, where the Airman also configures the NIDS.
2.example: A weather service gathers readings from stations across a region, studies them centrally and sends out warnings. In the course: a network-based intrusion detection system (NIDS) is required for monitoring activity on multiple systems, Block Text p.24.

3.summary: User settings are group policy configurations that apply to a user no matter which machine is used; they restrict user abilities on desktops.
3.deeper: Group policy lets network administrators change which Windows features are available to users and manage system security. A set of group policy configurations is called a group policy object (GPO). User settings follow the user to any machine. They include logon and logoff scripts, Internet Explorer settings such as favorites and the default home page, which Control Panel features users can change, which desktop icons appear and which items appear in the Start menu.
3.analogy: User settings are like a personal badge that carries the same access rules into any building the holder enters: the rules travel with the person, not with the building.
3.scenario: An Airman moves between several workstations during a shift. Because the restrictions are set as user settings, the same Control Panel limits, desktop icons and Start menu items appear on whichever machine the Airman logs on to.
3.example: A streaming account shows the same profile and parental limits on any screen where its owner signs in. User settings work the same way: they belong to the person, not the device. In the course: user settings apply to a user no matter which machine is used and are used to restrict user abilities on desktops, Block Text p.25.

3.summary: In a forward proxy, the client sends its request to the proxy server, which retrieves the resource out on the Internet and sends the response back to the client.
3.deeper: The forward proxy is the usual proxy: internal clients reach out to the Internet through it. A reverse proxy turns the direction around. It is used when a system on the Internet must send a request to one of your internal systems, such as a web server or mail server. The Internet system sends the request to the reverse proxy, which checks that the request is not malicious and then forwards it to the internal server. In both cases, all communication goes through the proxy.
3.analogy: A forward proxy is like a personal shopper you send out: you tell the shopper what you want, the shopper goes to the store and brings it back to you. A reverse proxy is like a receptionist who meets outside visitors and walks them to the right office.
3.scenario: An Airman at an internal workstation opens a web page. The request goes to the forward proxy, which fetches the page from the Internet and returns it. Later the Airman sees a different setup: a system on the Internet sends a request to the unit's internal web server through a reverse proxy.
3.example: Asking a friend who is going to the store to pick something up for you means the store deals only with your friend, who brings the item back. A forward proxy fetches resources for the client in a similar way. In the course: a forward proxy is where the client sends the request to the proxy server and the proxy retrieves the resource out on the Internet and sends the response to the client, Block Text p.27.

3.summary: An access control list (ACL) is built by setting permissions on files and folders so that only a specific group of users can access them, which maintains confidentiality.
3.deeper: ACLs come in three categories: File System ACLs, Active Directory ACLs and Networking ACLs. A File System ACL on a Windows server is set in two steps: secure the folder with NTFS permissions, then set share permissions when the folder is shared out to the network. A Networking ACL is set on a router: Cisco routers use access lists, standard or extended, to regulate traffic in and out of the network.
3.analogy: An ACL is like a guest list at a door: only the names on the list get in, so what is inside stays private to that group.
3.scenario: An Airman must keep a set of planning files readable only by one office. The Airman sets permissions on the folder so that only that office's group of users can reach it. The files stay confidential to that group.
3.example: A shared online photo album can be set so only invited family members can open it. Permissions on files and folders work the same way. In the course: implementing permissions on the files and folders is known as building an access control list (ACL), and allowing only a specific group of users access to the files maintains confidentiality, Block Text p.28.

3.summary: New Technology File System (NTFS) is the Windows file system with extra features, such as permissions, that a storage drive must have before its folders can get NTFS permissions.
3.deeper: All modern Windows systems should use NTFS rather than legacy file systems like FAT32, in part because NTFS has extra features such as permissions, which ACLs manage. To set NTFS permissions, the drive must first be formatted as NTFS; if it is not, it can be converted. Securing a folder on a Windows server takes two steps: secure the folder with NTFS permissions, then set share permissions when the folder is shared out. NTFS permissions apply when the user reaches the folder locally or across the network.
3.analogy: NTFS is like a filing cabinet with locks on each drawer: before you can hand out keys to drawers, the cabinet itself has to be the lockable kind.
3.scenario: An Airman finds that a storage drive uses FAT32 and cannot take the folder permissions the unit needs. The Airman converts the drive to NTFS, sets NTFS permissions on the folder, then shares the folder and sets share permissions.
3.example: A plain notebook cannot be locked, but a diary with a clasp can; to keep pages private you first need the kind that locks. NTFS is the format that makes permissions possible. 3.summary: Full Control is the NTFS folder or file permission that gives a user all permissions possible, including changing the file's permissions.
3.deeper: The common NTFS permissions build up: List Folder Contents lets a user view a folder's contents list; Read opens and reads files; Read and execute also runs executable files; Write modifies a file or creates a new file or folder; Modify includes all of these plus delete. Full Control gives every permission possible: the user can modify the contents of the file and also change its permissions.
3.analogy: Full Control is like holding the master key plus the right to cut new keys for others: you can open every door and also decide who else gets in.
3.scenario: An Airman with Modify can read, write and delete a file but cannot let a teammate open it. Only a user with Full Control can change the file's permissions.
3.example: On a shared online document, the owner can edit it and also decide who may view or edit; other editors can only change the text. Full Control is like the owner's role. In the course: Full Control is a folder or file permission that gives a user all permissions possible; the user will be able to modify the contents of the file and to change its permissions, Block Text p.28.

3.summary: Active Directory (AD) is a directory service that stores information about all network resources, such as servers, printers, user accounts, groups and security policies, across a domain.
3.deeper: AD is a directory service, not just a directory. Group policy can be configured on a local computer, or centrally for the network through Active Directory via Windows Server. Settings from Active Directory apply to systems and users every 90 minutes, on next logon and on restart.
3.analogy: Active Directory is like the central records office of a base: it holds the entry for every building, person, team and rule, so changes made there reach everyone.
3.scenario: MSgt Rush tells an Airman to apply one desktop policy to every system in the domain. Rather than set it on each computer, the Airman configures it centrally through Active Directory. The setting reaches systems within 90 minutes, at the next logon or on restart.
3.example: A school keeps one central office file listing every classroom, teacher, class group and school rule. Active Directory keeps that kind of central record for a network. In the course: Active Directory is a directory service that stores information about all network resources such as servers, printers, individual user accounts, groups of user accounts, security policies, and other information across a domain, Block Text p.29.

3.summary: A networking access control list is a set of rules on a router that regulates the traffic entering and leaving the network; Cisco routers use standard and extended access lists.
3.deeper: Like firewalls, routers can control what traffic can enter or leave the network. A standard access list is numbered 1 to 99 and permits or denies traffic based only on the source IP address. An extended access list is numbered 100 and above and can use the source and destination IP address and protocol information. Either list is configured in two steps: define the access list, then apply it to an interface on the router. The first rule that matches a packet is the rule the packet follows, and Cisco routers have an implicit deny rule at the bottom of the list by default.
3.analogy: An access list is like a checklist at a gate: the guard reads down the list and acts on the first line that fits the visitor; anyone who fits no line is turned away.
3.scenario: An Airman must stop traffic from one source address from entering the network. A standard access list can do it, because it filters only on the source IP address. The Airman defines the list, then applies it to the router interface.
3.example: A sorting machine checks each parcel against a list of rules from top to bottom and follows the first rule that fits; a parcel that fits no rule is set aside. A router access list works through its rules in a similar way. In the course: networking ACLs can be configured to regulate inbound and outbound traffic; Cisco routers have two common types of access lists, standard and extended, Block Text p.29.

3.summary: A software-based firewall, also called an application-based, host-based or personal firewall, is software installed on a single system to protect that one system.
3.deeper: There are two major classes of firewalls: software-based and hardware-based. A host-based firewall can be installed on any system, a computer or a server. Common features: block incoming traffic, block outgoing traffic, show notifications, a default rule of denying all traffic unless you allow it (implicit deny), and rules you add on top of the default rule. It can come from a third party or with the operating system; Windows includes Windows Firewall. A hardware-based (network-based) firewall instead sits at the edge of a network and controls traffic entering and leaving the network.
3.analogy: A software-based firewall is like the lock on one apartment door: it guards that one home, while a hardware firewall is like the guard at the building's front entrance.
3.scenario: An Airman needs protection on one server that sits alongside many other systems. The Airman installs a host-based firewall on that server. Once enabled, it denies all traffic until the Airman adds rules for the traffic the server needs.
3.example: A phone can have its own lock screen even when it is on a home network with a router. A software-based firewall is that kind of per-device protection. In the course: a software-based firewall is a piece of software that is installed on a single system to protect that one system, Block Text p.30.

3.summary: Notifications are a host-based firewall feature: the firewall can be configured to show a message when someone tries to connect to your system or a program on your system tries to send data out.
3.deeper: Most host-based firewalls can show such a message. It covers both directions: a connection attempt coming in to your system from the network or Internet, and a program on your system trying to send data out to the network or Internet. Windows Firewall has its own notification control: Change notification settings sets whether you wish to be notified when Windows Firewall blocks a program.
3.analogy: Notifications are like a doorbell camera that pings your phone: it tells you when someone tries the front door and when something tries to leave by it.
3.scenario: An Airman turns on notifications in the host-based firewall of a workstation. Later a message appears: a program on the workstation is trying to send data out to the Internet. Another message shows that someone on the network tried to connect to the workstation.
3.example: A banking app can send an alert each time someone tries to sign in to the account. A firewall notification gives that kind of alert for connections and outgoing data. In the course: most host-based firewalls can be configured to show a message if someone tries to connect to your system or if a program on your system tries to send data out on the network or Internet, Block Text p.30.

3.summary: Windows Firewall is the software-based firewall included with Windows operating systems.
3.deeper: Software-based firewalls can be installed from a third party or included with an operating system; Windows includes Windows Firewall. Its features: allow a program or feature through Windows Firewall; change notification settings; turn Windows Firewall on or off for specific network locations; restore defaults; and advanced settings, which let you control detailed inbound and outbound rules.

3.example: Many cars come with a built-in alarm, so the owner does not have to add one, and its settings can still be changed. Windows Firewall comes with the operating system in a similar way. In the course: Windows OSs include Windows Firewall, a software-based firewall, Block Text p.30.

4.summary: Security zones are the network segments that firewalls divide a network into for overall protection; a firewall plan typically creates three: the private zone, the DMZ and the public zone.
4.deeper: Firewalls allow a network administrator to divide a network into different segments, or zones. The private zone holds the LAN; the DMZ, between an external and an internal firewall, holds servers the public must reach; the public zone is any network the administrator does not control. Organizations often add zones, such as extranet, wireless and guest zones. The purpose of segmenting the network is to control communication between the zones.
4.analogy: Security zones are like the areas of an airport: the public hall, the checked gate area and the staff-only rooms, each separated by a checkpoint that controls who moves between them.
4.scenario: An Airman drafts a firewall plan. The workstations go in the private zone, the public web server goes in the DMZ, and the Internet is the public zone. The firewalls between them control what traffic may move from one zone to another.
4.example: A home may have a front yard anyone can walk past, a porch where delivery people may step, and the inside rooms for the family only, with a door between each. Security zones divide a network in a similar way. In the course: when creating your firewall plan you will typically create three security zones: private zone, demilitarized zone (DMZ), and the public zone, Block Text p.33.

4.summary: The intranet zone is another name for the private zone: the zone where the Local Area Network resides.
4.deeper: A firewall plan typically creates three security zones: the private zone, the demilitarized zone (DMZ) and the public zone. The private zone may also be called the private LAN or the intranet zone. The firewall placed in front of the private LAN ensures that no traffic from any other network is sent through the firewall to the private LAN.
4.analogy: The intranet zone is like the staff-only offices of a building: the firewall in front of it is a door that opens for no one coming from outside.
4.scenario: An Airman reads a firewall plan that names a "private LAN" in one place and an "intranet zone" in another. Both mean the same zone: the one where the unit's Local Area Network resides, behind a firewall that sends no traffic from other networks through to it.
4.example: A house may be called home, the residence or the house on different forms, but it is the same place. The private zone, private LAN and intranet zone are likewise one zone. 4.summary: The public zone is any network not controlled by the network administrator; the Internet is the best and most popular example.
4.deeper: The public zone is one of the three security zones a firewall plan typically creates, with the private zone and the DMZ. As a firewall administrator, you control which traffic comes from the public zone to the intranet zone.
4.analogy: The public zone is like the street outside a building: the building's managers do not run it, so they decide at their own doors who comes in from it.
4.scenario: An Airman lists the networks on a firewall plan. The Internet goes in the public zone, because the unit's network administrator does not control it. The Airman then sets which traffic from the public zone may come into the intranet zone.
4.example: A public road is used by everyone and run by no single homeowner, so each homeowner decides who may come up their own driveway. The public zone is that kind of network for a firewall plan. In the course: the public zone is any network not controlled by the network administrator, and the best and most popular example is the Internet, Block Text p.33.

4.summary: A wireless zone places the wireless network in a network zone of its own, so the firewall administrator can control which zones wireless clients can access.
4.deeper: Organizations often add zones to the usual three to create segments for different types of users. Extranet, wireless and guest zones are common. With the wireless network in its own zone, the firewall administrator can, for example, keep wireless clients from reaching the intranet or extranet zones. A guest zone is different: it is designed for visitors and gives access to the public Internet zone but to none of the other zones.
4.analogy: A wireless zone is like a separate waiting room for people who arrive by a side entrance: staff decide which doors from that room are unlocked.
4.scenario: MSgt Rush asks an Airman to add wireless access to the office without opening the private LAN to it. The Airman places the wireless network in its own zone, and the firewall administrator controls which zones wireless clients can reach, keeping them off the intranet and extranet zones.
4.example: A hotel may give its lobby a separate door to the pool, so lobby visitors can reach the pool but not the staff offices. A wireless zone gets its own controlled set of doors in a similar way. In the course: the wireless network could be placed in a network zone of its own, which gives the firewall administrator the opportunity to control which zones the wireless client can access, Block Text p.34.

5.summary: A computer incident response team (CIRT) is the incident response team: it knows how to handle security incidents in the organization, and it corrects and documents the security issues in a timely manner.
5.deeper: Having this team in place is the first thing to do to prepare for handling security incidents. The team is made up of different types of employees with different skill sets. The team leader makes sure every member knows their role and builds relationships with outside resources. Technical specialists assess the situation, identify its scale and know how to correct it. The documentation specialist logs each incident, its cause and its solution in a documentation database. The legal advisor knows the laws and regulations for computer forensics and incident response.
5.analogy: A CIRT is like a pit crew: each member has one job they know well. One keeps the crew coordinated, others do the repairs, one keeps the record of what was done, and one answers questions about the rules.
5.scenario: A security incident hits a unit’s servers. The team leader makes sure each member knows their role. A Linux specialist on the team assesses the scale of the incident and corrects it, the documentation specialist logs the cause and the solution, and when a legal question about computer forensics comes up, the team turns to the legal advisor.
5.example: In a hospital, a trauma team brings together people with different skills who each know their part when a patient arrives. A CIRT brings different skills together in the same way for security incidents. In the course: an incident response team is responsible for knowing how to handle security incidents that occur within the organization, and for correcting and documenting the security issues in a timely manner, Block Text p.35.

5.summary: The incident response plan is developed once the incident response team is in place. It identifies the different types of incidents and the job role of each team member during an incident.
5.deeper: Common elements of the plan are: Incident Categories, the types of security incidents that can occur; Roles and Responsibilities, each member’s job before, during and after an incident; Reporting Requirements/Escalation, when and how users report potential incidents, who the first responder is, and what the report should contain; Exercise Planning, practice from the identification phase through to the lessons learned; and User Roles, which names the first responder, the first individual notified, who takes charge of the incident.
5.analogy: The plan is like a team’s playbook written before the game: it names the situations that can come up, who does what in each, and how the team practices them.
5.scenario: After the CIRT is formed, an Airman helps write the incident response plan. It lists incident types such as a denial of service attack, sets each member’s role before, during and after an incident, tells users when and how to report, names the first responder, and schedules exercises so everyone is prepared for the day an incident occurs.
5.example: A school’s fire plan says what can happen, who leads each class out and how drills are practiced, all before any fire. An incident response plan does the same for security incidents. In the course: once the incident response team is in place, an incident response plan will be developed, which should identify different types of incidents and the job role of each team member during an incident, Block Text p.36.

5.summary: Incident categories are the different types of security incidents that can occur in an organization. The incident response plan should define them, for example a “social engineering attack” and a “denial of service attack.”
5.deeper: Defining incident categories is one of the common elements of the incident response plan. When a possible event or incident is investigated, it is given a category number that identifies it for descriptive purposes and for the level of severity of its potential impact to the mission, and reaction to different categories is different. Table 5-3 lists categories 0 to 9, such as CAT 1 Root-Level Intrusion, CAT 4 Denial of Service, CAT 7 Malicious Logic, CAT 8 Investigating and CAT 9 Explained Anomaly.
5.analogy: Incident categories work like the named sections of a filing cabinet: each problem goes into the section for its type, and each section has its own way of being handled.
5.scenario: MSgt Rush’s unit detects suspicious activity whose cause is not yet apparent, so it is categorized as CAT 8, Investigating. Further investigation shows that it was a system malfunction, so before closure it is re-categorized as CAT 9, Explained Anomaly.
5.example: A library sorts its books into named sections, so anyone can tell what kind of book each one is. Incident categories give names to the types of security incidents in the same way. In the course: the plan should define the different types of security incidents that can occur within your organization, Block Text p.36.

picture.alt: Part of Table 5-3, Event/Incident Categories: CAT 1, 4, 7, 8 and 9 with their type and name.

parts.label: CAT 1
parts.caption: Root-level intrusion: unauthorized access to information or credentials that could perform administrative functions, or malicious code that gives remote interactive control.

parts.label: CAT 4
parts.caption: Denial of service: activity that denies, degrades or disrupts normal functionality of an IS or DoD information network.

parts.label: CAT 7
parts.caption: Malicious logic: software installed by adversaries that does not give remote interactive control; with interactive access it is CAT 1 or CAT 2.

parts.label: CAT 8
parts.caption: Investigating: potentially malicious or anomalous events under further review. No event is closed out as CAT 8; it is re-categorized first.

parts.label: CAT 9
parts.caption: Explained anomaly: suspicious events found, after investigation, to be non-malicious, such as system malfunctions and false alarms.

5.summary: Roles and responsibilities is the element of the incident response plan that defines each team member’s job role before a security incident occurs, during it and after it.
5.deeper: The incident response plan should identify the job role of each team member during an incident, and the Roles and Responsibilities element defines those roles for before, during and after a security incident. The team leader is responsible for ensuring that all team members know their role when a security incident occurs. It is a different element from Incident Categories, which defines the types of incidents rather than who does what.
5.analogy: It is like a theater crew’s cue sheet, which says what each crew member does before the show, during it and after the curtain falls.
5.scenario: While the plan is written, an Airman sets down the job role of the documentation specialist before an incident, during the response and after it, and then does the same for every other member. When an incident occurs, the team leader can make sure each member knows their role.
5.example: In a relay race, each runner knows before the start which leg is theirs, what to do while running and what to do after the handoff. Roles and responsibilities set out each team member’s part in the same way. In the course: the plan should define each team member’s roles and responsibilities, including each member’s job role before a security incident occurs, during, and after a security incident, Block Text p.36.

5.summary: Reporting requirements/escalation is the element of the incident response plan that identifies when and how users report potential security incidents, who the first responder is to escalate to, and what the report should contain.
5.deeper: The plan should identify when and how users are supposed to report potential security incidents. It should also identify the first responder to escalate the incident to: the first individual notified, who takes charge of the incident and is a member of the incident response team. Finally, the plan identifies any reporting requirements for the incident and what elements the report should contain. Reporting accurate incident information as close to near-real-time as possible is crucial to an effective response.
5.analogy: It is like the hazard-reporting rules on a job site: they say when to speak up, who to tell first and what the report must say.
5.scenario: An Airman sees what may be a security incident on a workstation. Following the plan, the Airman reports it when and how the plan says, escalates it to the first responder the plan names, and makes sure the report holds the elements the plan requires.
5.example: Many buildings post a sign that says what to do if you see smoke: who to call and what to tell them. Reporting requirements give users that kind of guidance for security incidents. In the course: the plan should identify when and how users are supposed to report potential security incidents, Block Text p.36.

5.summary: The first responder is the first individual to be notified of an incident. The first responder takes charge of the incident and is a member of the incident response team.
5.deeper: The incident response plan identifies who the first responder is, so users know who to escalate an incident to. The primary goal of the first responder is to activate the CIRT and contain the incident. For example, if a virus is discovered on a system, the first responder should isolate the computer from the network by disconnecting the network cable. If systems on the network are replicating a worm out to the Internet, it may be necessary to power off the switch or disconnect from the Internet to stop the spread.
5.analogy: The first responder is like the first firefighter on the scene: they take charge, call in the rest of the crew and keep the fire from spreading.
5.scenario: MSgt Rush is the first person notified that a virus has been discovered on a workstation. As first responder, the sergeant takes charge, isolates the workstation by disconnecting its network cable, and activates the CIRT.
5.example: When someone falls ill in a store, the first trained person to arrive takes charge, keeps things from getting worse and calls for more help. The first responder plays that part for a security incident. In the course: the first responder is the first individual to be notified of the incident and takes charge of the incident, Block Text p.37.

questions.hint: Each time, think about stopping the spread and getting help.
questions.takeaway: The first responder contains the incident (isolate, or cut off the Internet) and activates the CIRT.

5.summary: An event is any observable occurrence in a system and/or network. Events sometimes provide indication that an incident is occurring.
5.deeper: Upon detection of a possible event by internal or external sources, the appropriate operations center (OC) and Air Force Cyberspace Defense (ACD) units initiate notification procedures. It must then be determined whether a detected event is a reportable event or incident, by assessing it against the incident criteria. In Table 5-3 each category is marked as an event or as an incident: for example, CAT 0 Training and Exercises and CAT 8 Investigating are events.
5.analogy: An event is like any sound a night guard hears: most are harmless, but some are a sign that something is wrong and need a closer look.
5.scenario: An IDS sensor records repeated attempts to log in with possible username and password combinations, and normal defensive mechanisms defeat them. That observable occurrence is an event: CAT 3, Unsuccessful Activity Attempt. It is still assessed against the incident criteria.
5.example: A smoke detector chirping is something anyone can notice; sometimes it means a fire, often it means nothing at all. An event is any such observable occurrence. In the course: an event is any observable occurrence in a system and/or network, Block Text p.37.

picture.alt: An event is detected, assessed against the incident criteria, and found to be a reportable event or an incident.

steps.caption: An event is any observable occurrence in a system and/or network.

answers.text: An incident, because every observable occurrence jeopardizes confidentiality, integrity or availability

CAT 1 needs a finding of unauthorized access to administrative credentials or information, or remote interactive control; nothing has been found yet.

questions.stem: Table 5-3 marks each category as an event or an incident. Sort these categories.

items.text: CAT 4 Denial of Service

items.why: Table 5-3 marks CAT 6 as an event: it gathers information and does not directly result in a compromise.

items.text: CAT 7 Malicious Logic

5.summary: An incident is an assessed occurrence that actually or potentially jeopardizes the confidentiality, integrity or availability of an information system or the information it processes, stores or transmits, or that violates or imminently threatens security policies, security procedures or acceptable use policies.
5.deeper: An event is any observable occurrence; an incident is an occurrence that has been assessed and meets this definition. A detected event is assessed against the incident criteria to decide whether it is a reportable event or incident. When the cause or intent of a possible event is not readily apparent, it is first categorized as CAT 8, Investigating, and no event is closed out as CAT 8: it is re-categorized before closure. As the investigation progresses, the category may change, for example from CAT 8 to a root-level intrusion (CAT 1 incident).
5.analogy: An event is like a cough; an incident is what a doctor’s exam confirms as a real or likely illness. The exam, the assessment, is what turns an observation into an incident.
5.scenario: A sensor flags activity whose intent is not clear, so it is categorized as CAT 8 while the ACD unit gathers system logs and IDS logs. The data shows unauthorized access to account credentials that could perform administrative functions, so the event is re-designated as a root-level intrusion, a CAT 1 incident.
5.example: A store alarm going off is only a signal until someone checks and finds a broken window and missing goods. An incident is the checked occurrence that shows real or potential harm. In the course: an incident is an assessed occurrence that actually or potentially jeopardizes the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of an information system, Block Text p.37.

picture.alt: A detected event of unclear cause is categorized CAT 8, investigated, assessed against the incident criteria and re-categorized.

steps.caption: A possible event is detected, but its cause or intent is not readily apparent.
It is first categorized as a CAT 8 investigation. No event is closed out as CAT 8.
The ACD unit gathers data such as system logs and IDS and IPS logs, and the event is assessed against the incident criteria.
As information is obtained, the category may change: an initial CAT 8 event may be re-designated a root-level intrusion (CAT 1 incident).

5.summary: The incident handling process is the standard set of six phases followed in response to cyber incidents, according to Air Force instruction (AFI) 17-203, Cyber Incident Handling.
5.deeper: The phases are Detection and Reporting of Events, Preliminary Analysis and Identification, Preliminary Response Actions, Incident Analysis, Response and Recovery, and Post-Incident Analysis. An investigation involving law enforcement or criminal investigation, or the nature and sensitivity of an operation, may cause a deviation from the typical process; otherwise the six phases are followed. Steps and terminology for the industry at large are slightly different than for the USAF.
5.analogy: It is like a hospital case: the problem is noticed, sorted, stabilized, examined closely, treated, and finally the staff review how the case was handled.
5.scenario: Sensors detect suspicious activity and it is reported. The OC and ACD units categorize it and send notifications. Technicians contain the threat and preserve the data. Analysts work out the root cause, the local CFP’s POA&M guides restoration, and a postmortem records lessons learned.
5.example: A fire crew answers each call with the same set of steps: take the alarm, size up the scene, contain the fire, find the cause, clean up, then review the call. The incident handling process is such a set of steps for cyber incidents. In the course: the standard six phases are the steps taken in response to cyber incidents according to AFI 17-203, Cyber Incident Handling, Block Text p.39.

picture.alt: The six phases of the incident handling process (AFI 17-203), from detection to post-incident analysis.

steps.caption: Detection and reporting of events: through IDS/IPS sensors, EITSM records, trend analysis and problem management; accurate, real-time reports are crucial.
Preliminary analysis and identification: the OC and ACD units start notification procedures and categorize the activity.
Preliminary response actions: immediate steps once an incident is declared: contain the threat and preserve the data.
Incident analysis: find out what occurred, including the technical details, root cause(s) and potential impact.
Response and recovery: prevent further damage, restore integrity; the local CFP develops a POA&M.
Post-incident analysis: a postmortem reviews how effective and efficient the incident handling was.

questions.stem: Right after an incident is declared, technicians contain the threat and make primary and working images of affected systems. Which phase is this?

answers.why: This phase detects activity and reports it; containment comes once an incident has been declared.
Preliminary response actions are the immediate steps once an incident is declared: contain the threat and safely acquire and preserve data, including images of affected systems.
Response and recovery are the detailed steps that restore integrity and prevent recurrence, guided by the POA&M; they come after incident analysis.
Post-incident analysis is the postmortem review of how the incident was handled, at the end.

questions.hint: Look for the phase of immediate steps taken before the detailed analysis.
questions.takeaway: Preliminary response actions contain the threat and preserve data right after an incident is declared.

5.summary: Preliminary analysis and identification is phase 2 of the incident handling process: the operations center (OC) and Air Force Cyberspace Defense (ACD) units initiate notification procedures and categorize the activity.
5.deeper: The OC and ACD units initiate notification procedures in accordance with AFI 10-206, CJCSM 6510.01B and the established SOPs of the affected units, and notification messages must be properly classified. Analysis and identification is primarily accomplished and categorized from these organizational positions. As the investigation progresses and more information is obtained, the assigned category may change to reflect the new data: an initial CAT 8 event may be re-designated as a root-level intrusion (CAT 1 incident) or as non-compliance activity (CAT 5 event). Containing the threat and preserving data come in the next phase, preliminary response actions.
5.analogy: It is like a dispatch center after an emergency call: it alerts the right people, gives the call a first label, and changes the label as more is learned.
5.scenario: Activity is reported, and the OC and ACD units send properly classified notification messages. Its cause is not clear, so it is categorized as CAT 8. Further information shows that an authorized user failed to apply security patches, so the category is changed to non-compliance activity, a CAT 5 event.
5.example: At a hospital front desk, a new patient gets a first label and the right staff are alerted; the label changes once the doctors learn more. Preliminary analysis and identification does this for detected activity. In the course: the appropriate operations center (OC) and Air Force Cyberspace Defense (ACD) units will initiate notification procedures, and analysis and identification is primarily accomplished and categorized from these organizational positions, Block Text p.39.

picture.alt: Phase 2: the operations center and the ACD unit send notification messages, categorize the activity and change its category as information comes in.

steps.caption: The appropriate operations center (OC) and Air Force Cyberspace Defense (ACD) units initiate notification procedures under AFI 10-206, CJCSM 6510.01B and the units’ SOPs.
Notification messages must be properly classified.
Analysis and identification is primarily accomplished and categorized from these positions; activity of unclear cause starts as CAT 8.
As the investigation progresses, the category may change, for example to a root-level intrusion (CAT 1 incident) or non-compliance activity (CAT 5 event).

5.summary: Incident analysis is the series of analytical steps taken to find out what happened in an incident, including the identification of its root cause.
5.deeper: Incident analysis is phase 4 of the incident handling process, and it is performed while an event is still in progress. The mission owner is included. Its purpose is to understand the technical details, root cause(s) and potential impact of the incident, which helps decide what more information to gather, how to coordinate information sharing, and how to work with the MAJCOM and others to develop a course of action. Under AFI 17-203 it has five steps: gather information, validate the incident, determine the operational impact, coordinate, and determine reporting requirements.
5.analogy: It is like an accident investigator at a crash: collect the facts, check them, judge the damage, bring in the right people, then decide who must be told.
5.scenario: While an incident is still in progress, an Airman collects external logs and personal accounts, checks that the reported incident is accurate, judges how it affects the mission, works with the system’s owning CFP on its Mission Assurance Category level, and then determines within one hour whether OPREP-3 reporting applies.
5.example: When a car will not start, a mechanic first hears what the owner saw, checks it, decides how serious it is, and only then decides who needs to be told. Incident analysis takes that kind of step-by-step look at an incident. In the course: incident analysis is the series of analytical steps taken to find out what happened in an incident, Block Text p.41.

picture.alt: The five steps of incident analysis under AFI 17-203.

steps.caption: Gather information: all involved personnel identify and collect all relevant information about the incident.
Validate the incident: continuously review, corroborate and update the reported incident to ensure accuracy.
Determine the operational impact: the detrimental impacts on the organization’s ability to perform its mission.
Coordinate with the victim system’s owning CFP, the NOSC and the MCCC to determine its Mission Assurance Category level.
Determine reporting requirements: within one hour, decide whether OPREP-3 or CCIR reporting requirements are met.

5.summary: Gather information is step 1 of incident analysis: all involved personnel identify and collect all relevant information about the incident for use in the analysis.
5.deeper: The information gathered may include data previously acquired and preserved, external logs, personal accounts, all-source intelligence, technical information, or the current operational situation. The next step, validating the incident, then reviews, corroborates and updates the reported incident to ensure the accuracy of all information.
5.analogy: It is like a detective’s first visit to a scene: collect every clue before trying to explain what happened.
5.scenario: An incident is still in progress. Every involved person collects relevant information: images preserved earlier, external logs, personal accounts from users, all-source intelligence and the current operational situation. The team then checks it for accuracy in the next step.
5.example: Before a doctor decides anything, the staff collect the patient’s history, earlier test results and the patient’s own account. Gathering information is that first collection for an incident. In the course: all involved personnel should identify and collect all relevant information about the incident for use in incident analysis, Block Text p.41.

5.summary: Operational impact refers to detrimental impacts on an organization’s ability to perform its mission.
5.deeper: Operational impact may include direct and/or indirect effects that diminish or incapacitate system or network capabilities, the compromise and/or loss of mission critical data, or the temporary or permanent loss of mission critical applications or systems. Determining it is step 3 of incident analysis. For help preparing an impact assessment, coordinate as necessary with the HQ USAF Damage Assessment Management Office (AF-DAMO), the lead CDA unit for Cyber Operations Risk Assessments (CORA), or other organizations.
5.analogy: It is like judging storm damage to a farm not by broken boards but by whether the farm can still bring in its harvest.
5.scenario: Malicious logic takes a mission critical application offline for a day. In step 3 of incident analysis, an Airman records that temporary loss of a mission critical application as operational impact, and coordinates with AF-DAMO for help preparing the impact assessment.
5.example: When a delivery company’s trucks break down, what matters most is how many deliveries it can no longer make. Operational impact measures harm by the mission it stops. In the course: operational impact refers to detrimental impacts on an organization’s ability to perform its mission, Block Text p.41.

parts.label: Data

parts.label: Applications

5.summary: Coordinate is step 4 of incident analysis: work with the victim system’s owning CFP, the network operations and security center (NOSC) and the mission control center (MCCC), as appropriate, to determine the Mission Assurance Category level of the system.
5.deeper: Coordinate comes after the operational impact is determined (step 3) and before reporting requirements are determined (step 5). The organizations it works with are tied to the victim system: its owning communications focal point (CFP), the NOSC and, as appropriate, the MCCC. What it sets out to determine is the system’s Mission Assurance Category level.
5.analogy: It is like a repair crew checking with a building’s owners and managers to learn how critical that building is before taking the next steps.
5.scenario: The operational impact of an incident on a server has been determined. Next, an Airman coordinates with the server’s owning CFP and the NOSC, and with the MCCC as appropriate, to determine the server’s Mission Assurance Category level.
5.example: Before fixing a broken machine on a factory line, a technician asks the people who run it how important it is to their work. The Coordinate step asks a system’s owners a question of that kind. In the course: coordinate with the victim system’s owning CFP, network operations and security center (NOSC) and mission control center MCCC (as appropriate) to determine the Mission Assurance Category level of the system, Block Text p.41.

5.summary: Courses of action (COAs) are the planned responses to an incident. A postmortem captures problems with executing them, and its results can lead to revising existing COAs, figuring out why COAs failed, or creating new COAs.
5.deeper: Incident analysis helps the unit work with the MAJCOM and other organizations to develop a course of action for response and prevention. Under the COA heading, the ACD unit drafts a cyber incident report (CIR) with the affected systems, probable attackers, attack vectors used, and technical and operational impact (if known); the 25AF supports it with a network intelligence report (NIR). Data captured in the postmortem includes lessons learned, initial root cause, problems with executing COAs, missing policies and procedures, and inadequate infrastructure defenses. The results go to the affected MAJCOM/unit for corrective actions.
5.analogy: It is like a coach’s game plan: after the game, the team reviews what went wrong, then revises the plays, works out why one failed, or draws up new ones.
5.scenario: After an incident, the postmortem shows that a COA could not be carried out because a procedure was missing. The results go to the affected unit, which figures out why the COA failed and revises it.
5.example: After a fire drill goes badly, a school reviews what happened and rewrites its exit routes. Courses of action are revised in a similar way after a postmortem. In the course: corrective actions could include revising existing COAs, figuring out why the COAs failed, or creating new COAs, Block Text p.42.

picture.alt: From the cyber incident report to the postmortem and the corrective actions on courses of action (COAs).

6.summary: Cyber hygiene refers to the practices and steps that maintain system health and improve online security.
6.deeper: These practices are part of a routine to ensure identity safety and other details that could be compromised. Much like physical hygiene, cyber hygiene is regularly conducted to ward off natural deterioration and common threats, and secure network user habits ensure the cyber hygiene of the network. Cybersecurity experts estimate that 90% of cyber-attacks could be defeated by basic cyber hygiene and sharing best practices. Some habits belong to users, such as letting scans and updates run; others belong to administrators, such as managing firewalls and scanning all devices centrally.
6.analogy: Cyber hygiene is like brushing your teeth: small routine habits, done regularly, keep common problems from building up.
6.scenario: An Airman’s computer prompts for an antivirus update and a restart. The Airman allows the update, restarts, and lets the security scan run without interfering, while the network administrators keep the firewall settings out of users’ reach.
6.example: Washing your hands every day keeps common germs away without any big effort. Cyber hygiene is that kind of everyday routine for systems. In the course: cyber hygiene refers to the practices and steps that maintain system health and improve online security, Block Text p.43.

6.summary: Virus definitions are the updates antivirus software needs to be effective: updated virus definitions should be regularly pushed out to users to protect their systems.
6.deeper: An organization’s administrators should enforce standardized antivirus software installation across the network. For the software to be effective, updated virus definitions are pushed out regularly. Users should allow their software to perform automatic updates and should install and restart their machine when prompted. It is also important for users to maintain updated antivirus protection on their personal devices.
6.analogy: Virus definitions are like the latest forecast for a weather app: the app is only useful when it keeps receiving updates.
6.scenario: Administrators have standardized the antivirus software on every workstation. When updated virus definitions are pushed out, an Airman’s machine prompts to install and restart. The Airman allows the update and restarts, so the antivirus software stays effective.
6.example: A map app on a phone needs its updates to stay useful; without them it falls behind. Antivirus software needs updated virus definitions in a similar way. In the course: for antivirus software to be effective, updated virus definitions should be regularly pushed out to users to protect their systems, Block Text p.44.

6.summary: A password protects an account. It should be long and complex: at least 18 characters, a mix of numbers, symbols, capital and lower-case letters, and no dictionary word.
6.deeper: On the Air Force network most users use their common access card (CAC) paired with a PIN, but many systems and websites require usernames and passwords. The industry recommendation is a minimum of 18 characters (longer is better); numbers, symbols, capital and lower-case letters; no word that would be in a dictionary; and no obvious substitutions, such as replacing a single letter of a dictionary word with a number. A random strong password that must be saved to a document or written down is not secure, so use a word trick you will remember or a secure password program, and do not use the same password for multiple services.
6.analogy: A password is like the combination of a lock: the more dials and the more symbols on each dial, the harder it is for anyone to guess.
6.scenario: An Airman picks a common dictionary word and swaps one letter for a number. That substitution is obvious and easy to crack, so the Airman instead uses a mix of numbers, symbols and capital and lower-case letters at least 18 characters long, and keeps it in a secure password program rather than on paper.
6.example: A bike lock with only a few digits is easy to open by trying combinations. A longer, mixed password is like a lock with many more digits. In the course: you should create and maintain long and complex passwords to protect your accounts, Block Text p.44.

6.summary: A master password is the single password that protects an encrypted password-management wallet. It should be long and strong, and it should not be duplicated on other accounts.
6.deeper: Using the same password for multiple services is risky: if a single website is compromised, the password is at risk no matter how strong it is, and if all accounts use it, all the data is compromised. Personal password-management software handles the legwork of creating and using passwords. These secure wallets are encrypted and protected by a single master password. A strong random password saved to a document or written down is not secure, which is one reason to use such a program.
6.analogy: A master password is like the key to a lockbox holding all your other keys: it must be the hardest key to copy, and it opens no other lock.
6.scenario: An Airman has many website accounts and reuses one password on all of them. MSgt Rush points out that one compromised site would put every account at risk. The Airman gives each account its own password, keeps them in a password-management wallet, and protects the wallet with a long, strong master password used nowhere else.
6.example: A building manager keeps every apartment key in one locked key box, and the key to the box is the one guarded most closely. A master password is the key to that box. In the course: these secure wallets are encrypted and protected by a single master password, which should be long and strong as well and should not be duplicated on other accounts, Block Text p.44.

6.summary: The baseline configuration is the starting point for all future baseline assessments. It is created when the system is initially created and represents how the system is supposed to be configured.
6.deeper: As time goes on and updates are applied, the baseline configuration must be updated to keep it current. Baselining is the measuring of a system’s current state of security readiness, with tools that look for weaknesses such as default passwords and permission issues. It works simply: set up a system, measure the baseline, fix the issues, and declare the resulting configuration the baseline; after changes, measure again and look for deviations. A deviation can be positive (lower risk) or negative (higher risk); an increase in risk is evaluated for possible remediation.
6.analogy: A baseline is like a “before” photo of a room: after each change you compare the room with the photo to see what is different.
6.scenario: An Airman builds a new server, runs a scan that finds default passwords, fixes them and declares that configuration the baseline. After a patch, the Airman measures again and finds a deviation that increases risk, so the new risk level is evaluated for possible remediation.
6.example: At a first checkup, a doctor records a patient’s normal readings and compares every later visit with them. A baseline configuration is that first record for a system. In the course: the baseline configuration is the starting point for all future baseline assessments, Block Text p.46.

6.summary: Configuration management is the process for maintaining computer systems, servers and software in a reliable, consistent state, so a system continues to perform as expected while changes are made over time.
6.deeper: It is the discipline of ensuring all current and future software and hardware modifications to assets are always known and tracked, which prevents network changes from going undocumented. Misconfigurations can lead to poor performance, inconsistencies and noncompliance, and undocumented changes across many systems lead to instability and downtime. Maintaining the baseline lets a system be reverted. Proper tools classify systems by groups, centrally modify base configurations, roll out new settings to all applicable systems, automate patches and updates, identify outdated or noncompliant configurations, prioritize actions and apply prescriptive remediation.
6.analogy: Configuration management is like a car’s service log: every change is written down, so the car keeps running as expected and anyone can tell what was done.
6.scenario: Several administrators change settings on many servers without writing anything down, and the network becomes unstable. With configuration management, each change is documented and tracked, new settings are rolled out to all applicable systems, and the documentation lets the team restore the most recent functional settings.
6.example: A household that writes down every repair and change to its home can always tell what was done and undo a bad change. Configuration management keeps that kind of record for systems. In the course: configuration management is the process for maintaining computer systems, servers, and software in a reliable, consistent state, Block Text p.47.

6.summary: Disaster recovery is the first benefit of well-implemented configuration management: in the event of a disaster, assets are easily recoverable, and it is easy to roll back to the previous configuration that worked.
6.deeper: Well-implemented configuration management has three beneficial outcomes. Benefit 1 is disaster recovery: assets are easily recoverable, and the same applies to rollbacks. Benefit 2 is uptime and site reliability: site reliability refers to service availability, and any causes of downtime must be investigated and remediated. Benefit 3 is scalability: because the state of all services is known, provisioning, adding more resources such as servers, becomes a non-event.
6.analogy: Disaster recovery is like a saved game: when something goes wrong, you load the last save that worked instead of starting over.
6.scenario: An update leaves a server in a bad state. Because configuration management tracked the server’s configuration, an Airman rolls it back to the previous configuration that worked, and its assets are easily recovered.
6.example: A word processor’s undo history lets you go back to the version of a document that was fine. Configuration management gives systems a way back of that kind. In the course: in the event of a disaster, configuration management ensures that assets are easily recoverable, Block Text p.48.

6.summary: Redundant Array of Independent Disks (RAID) is a way to manage disk redundancy so that one logical drive is created from two or more physical drives in a safer and faster way.
6.deeper: There are five commonly used RAID configurations. RAID 0 stripes data across two drives for performance, with no redundancy. RAID 1 mirrors the data, so each drive duplicates the other. RAID 1+0 combines striping and mirroring and needs at least four disks, an even number. RAID 5 uses striping with a single parity bit, so there is one redundant disk, and needs at least three disks. RAID 6 uses striping with double parity, so there are two redundant disks, and needs at least four.
6.analogy: RAID is like several small bookshelves joined so they act as one big shelf, arranged so the books are reached faster, kept in two places, or both.
6.scenario: An Airman must set up storage for an email archive server. With RAID 5, data is striped with parity, so if one drive crashes the parity bits and the remaining data rebuild the lost data. The Airman uses at least three disks.
6.example: Several storage bins stacked and labeled as one cabinet can be used as if they were one piece of furniture. RAID makes two or more physical drives act as one logical drive. In the course: RAID is a way to manage disk redundancy so that you can create one logical drive from two or more physical drives in a safer and faster way, Block Text p.50.

6.summary: Striping stores data simultaneously to two physical drives, with portions of the data divided between the drives. It boosts performance.
6.deeper: Striping is the method of RAID 0. Because RAID 0 has no redundancy, it is not suitable for data drives: if one drive fails, all the data is permanently lost. RAID 0 needs at least two drives and is commonly used for voice and video streaming. Striping is also part of RAID 1+0, combined with mirroring, and of RAID 5 and RAID 6, which add parity so lost data can be rebuilt.
6.analogy: Striping is like two people each copying half of a book at the same time: the job goes faster, but if one person’s half is lost, the book is incomplete.
6.scenario: A voice and video streaming server needs performance, so an Airman uses RAID 0 striping across two drives. For a data drive whose data must be kept, the Airman would not use RAID 0 alone, because one failed drive means all the data is lost.
6.example: Two cashiers working the same line split the customers between them, so the line moves faster. Striping splits data between drives in a similar way. In the course: data is stored simultaneously to two physical drives, with portions of the data being divided between the two drives; this method is called striping, and it boosts performance, Block Text p.50.

6.summary: RAID 1 is called mirroring: all data that is saved to one drive is reflected on the other, giving the system a built-in backup.
6.deeper: Each drive is an exact duplicate of every other drive in the RAID 1 configuration. RAID 1 works very well for data drives where retention of the data is important. The minimum number of drives is two, and RAID 1 is commonly used for authentication servers. It differs from RAID 0, striping, which boosts performance but has no redundancy: if one RAID 0 drive fails, all the data is permanently lost.
6.analogy: RAID 1 is like writing your notes in two notebooks at once: if one notebook is lost, the other has every page.
6.scenario: An authentication server must not lose its data. An Airman sets it up with RAID 1 on two drives, so everything saved to one drive is reflected on the other. When one drive fails, the other still holds an exact duplicate.
6.example: Keeping a second, identical copy of a house key means losing one key does not lock you out. RAID 1 keeps a second identical drive in a similar way. In the course: RAID 1 is called mirroring, because all data that is saved to one drive is reflected on the other giving the system a built in back up, Block Text p.50.

6.summary: A full backup backs up all files and folders. It does not rely on the archive bit to tell it what to back up, but it does clear the bit as each file is backed up.
6.deeper: Most backups rely on archive bits (flags): an archive bit is a single binary digit within a file, where 1 means the file has not been backed up and 0 means it has. The full backup and the incremental backup clear the archive bit; differential backups do not. Restoring a full backup recovers all data that may have been lost. An incremental backup, by contrast, backs up only data changed since the previous backup, and restoring it needs the full backup first.
6.analogy: A full backup is like photocopying an entire binder instead of only the pages that changed.
6.scenario: An Airman runs a full backup of a file server. Every file and folder is copied, whether its archive bit is 1 or 0, and each file’s bit is cleared as it is backed up. When the server’s data is later lost, restoring the full backup recovers all of it.
6.example: Packing every item in a house for a move, not only the new ones, means everything ends up in the boxes. A full backup copies everything in a similar way. In the course: this backup type backs up all files and folders and does not rely on the archive bit to tell it what to backup, Block Text p.51.

6.summary: An incremental backup backs up all data that has changed since the previous backup, and it clears the archive bit.
6.deeper: Incremental backups are relatively fast because less data is backed up each time than with full and differential backups. They take more time to restore: the full backup must be restored first, followed by every incremental backup in the order they were made. Daily backups are normally incremental backups. Differential backups, by contrast, back up everything that has changed since the most recent full backup and do not clear the archive bit.
6.analogy: An incremental backup is like a diary that records only what happened each day: quick to write, but to know the whole story you read from the start through every entry in order.
6.scenario: A server gets a full backup, then an incremental backup each day after that. When the server crashes, an Airman restores the full backup first, then each daily incremental backup in the order they were made.
6.example: Copying only each night’s new photos to a drive is quick, but rebuilding the whole album means starting with the first big copy and adding each night’s batch in order. Incremental backups work in a similar way. In the course: incremental backups backup all data that has changed since the previous backup, Block Text p.52.

6.summary: A disaster recovery plan (DRP) is the IT plan every department should develop, with step-by-step instructions on what is to be done when a disaster strikes.
6.deeper: The plan begins by compiling an inventory of hardware, software applications and data, and includes a strategy to ensure that all critical information is backed up. It defines the critical systems, the disaster recovery team with contact details, the recovery time objective (RTO), communication methods, an alternative facility and a master list of inventories. The planning steps are: assemble a disaster recovery team, perform risk assessments, prioritize processes and operations, collect data, create the plan, and test it. Tests include walk-throughs, tabletop exercises, functional exercises and full-scale exercises.
6.analogy: A DRP is like a family’s emergency plan: who is in charge, what could happen, what matters most, where everything is, the written plan itself, and practice drills.
6.scenario: A department forms a disaster recovery team with core members from all departments and top management. It analyzes possible natural and man-made disasters, orders its operations from critical to non-essential, collects contact details and backup storage locations, writes the plan in a standard format, and then tests it with a tabletop exercise.
6.example: Before a big storm, a family agrees who leads, what could go wrong, what to save first and where the supplies are, writes it down and practices it. A DRP does this for IT systems. In the course: all departments should develop an IT disaster recovery plan, which begins by compiling an inventory of hardware, software applications, and data, Block Text p.52.

Create the plan in a standard format, with step-by-step instructions for when a disaster strikes.

7.summary: Computer Security (COMPUSEC) is the Air Force program that protects all Air Force information system resources and information, with a focus on end-point security and ports, protocols and services management.
7.deeper: COMPUSEC compliance ensures that measures to protect Air Force information systems (ISs) and their information are put in place properly. Its objective is to employ countermeasures that protect the confidentiality, integrity and availability of government information processed by Air Force ISs. It includes all measures that safeguard ISs and information against sabotage, tampering, denial of service, espionage, fraud, misappropriation, misuse, or release to unauthorized persons. Air Force Manual (AFMAN) 17-1301 implements the program. It applies to all Air Force information technology used to process, store, display, transmit or protect Air Force information, whatever its classification or sensitivity, unless exempted through the risk management framework process. Success needs adequate training and proper use of cybersecurity resources.
7.analogy: COMPUSEC is like the rule book and guard duty for every computer in a unit at once: one manual sets the rules, the rules cover every machine whatever it holds, and named people answer for following them.
7.scenario: An Airman asks whether COMPUSEC covers a system that only handles unclassified information. It does: COMPUSEC applies to all Air Force information technology, regardless of classification or sensitivity, unless the system was exempted through the risk management framework process. The Information System Security Officer and other privileged cybersecurity personnel answer for compliance.
7.example: A building has one safety program that covers every room, from the storeroom to the main office, and a written manual that says how. COMPUSEC works the same way for Air Force computers. In the course: COMPUSEC compliance ensures appropriate implementation of measures to protect all Air Force information system resources and information, Block Text p.54.

7.summary: The CIA Triad is the name for the three fundamental goals of information security taken together: confidentiality, integrity and availability.
7.deeper: As an information technology professional, an Airman works to reach the fundamental goals of information security: confidentiality, integrity and availability. Together they are called the CIA Triad, which is not to be confused with the Central Intelligence Agency. Confidentiality means only authorized persons can gain access to information and read it. Integrity means data has not been altered in transit or in storage. Availability means the information is there when the user wants it. The COMPUSEC objective is to employ countermeasures that protect all three for government information processed by Air Force information systems.
7.analogy: The triad is like a three-legged stool, with one leg each for secrecy, accuracy and being there when needed.
7.scenario: An Airman reviews three changes: file permissions so only one team can read a report, a hash check on a downloaded program, and regular backups of critical data. Each change serves a different goal of the CIA Triad: confidentiality, integrity and availability.
7.example: A bank vault keeps money away from strangers, keeps the count right, and opens when the customer needs the money. The CIA Triad asks the same three things of information. In the course: those fundamental goals are confidentiality, integrity, and availability, collectively termed the CIA Triad, Block Text p.55.

7.summary: Confidentiality is the goal that only authorized persons can gain access to information and read it; permissions and encryption help keep information confidential.
7.deeper: Permissions on files and folders make sure only the right user accounts can reach a file. They are not sufficient alone: most organizations keep information on a server, and when users download files across the network, permissions do not protect the contents in transit. Encryption puts information in an unreadable format until an authorized person decrypts it. Files can be encrypted in storage, so the data stays unreadable even if a hacker with physical access gets around the permissions, or in transit, by encrypting the communications channel so someone who taps into it cannot read the data. Steganography, hiding information in a graphic file, is another way to conceal information.
7.analogy: Confidentiality is like a sealed letter in a locked mailbox: the lock decides who reaches it, and the seal keeps it private even while it is carried.
7.scenario: An Airman sets permissions so only one office can open a set of files on the server. Users will also download the files to their computers, so the Airman encrypts the communications channel too. The permissions decide who gets the files; the encryption keeps the contents unreadable on the way.
7.example: A diary with a lock is meant to be read only by its owner. Confidentiality is the same goal for information. In the course: one of the goals of information security is to ensure confidentiality such that only authorized persons can gain access to information and are able to read the information, Block Text p.55.

7.summary: Access control means setting permissions on files and folders so that only a specific group of users can reach them; building these permissions is building an access control list (ACL).
7.deeper: Most network administrators secure information on the network by putting permissions on files and folders. Because the administrator is controlling who can access the files, this is called building an access control list (ACL). Allowing only a specific group of users to reach the files helps maintain confidentiality. Permissions alone are not enough: they make sure only the right user accounts can get to a file, but once a user downloads the file across the network, the permissions do not protect its contents while it is in transit. That is where encryption comes in.
7.analogy: An ACL is like a guest list at a door: only the names on the list get in. The list guards the door, though, not what a guest carries out once inside.
7.scenario: An Airman sets permissions on a shared folder so that only one work group can open its files. That builds an access control list and helps keep the files confidential. When a group member downloads a file to a client computer, the permissions no longer protect the contents on the way, so encryption is needed for the transfer.
7.example: A locked cabinet with a list of who holds a key keeps papers away from everyone else in the office. Access control does the same for files. In the course: by setting permissions on the files and allowing only a specific group of users access to the files, you are helping to maintain confidentiality, Block Text p.55.

7.summary: Steganography is a method of hiding information, such as a text file, in a graphic file, to keep it confidential.
7.deeper: The information is placed in the graphic file using a program, and a password is placed on the file. After the graphic is sent to the intended receiver, the receiver uses the steganography application to read the information out of the file. Steganography is also used by people with malicious motives to send hidden information: a group of hackers could hide text files about their next plot in the pictures of a normal-looking web site, and the other members download the graphics and extract the text files.
7.analogy: Steganography is like writing a note inside a picture frame, behind the photo. Anyone sees only the picture; the person who knows where to look takes out the note.
7.scenario: An Airman notices that a group shares ordinary-looking pictures on a web site, and members download the graphics and run a program on them. The group is using steganography: text files hidden in the graphics are extracted with the steganography program.
7.example: A greeting card can carry a second message under a flap that only the receiver knows to lift. Steganography hides information inside a picture file in the same spirit. In the course: steganography is a method of hiding information, such as a text file, in a graphic file, Block Text p.55.

7.summary: Integrity is the goal that data sent from a source arrives at its destination, or sits in storage, without having been altered.
7.deeper: Data integrity is not personal integrity or ethics. To check integrity over a network, the sending system runs the data through a hashing algorithm, which generates a hash value that is sent with the data. The destination runs the data through the same algorithm and compares its own hash value with the one sent; if they are the same, the data is assumed not altered. Vendors often give the hash value of a download so users can do their own integrity check. A digital signature, made with a person’s private key, proves the sender is who they say they are, and nonrepudiation, through digital signatures or auditing, means someone cannot dispute sending a message or making a change.
7.analogy: Integrity is like counting the items in a box before it ships and again when it arrives: if both counts match, nothing was taken or added on the way.
7.scenario: An Airman downloads a program, and the vendor lists the file’s hash value. The Airman runs the same check on the downloaded file. The two hash values match, so the file was not altered during the download.
7.example: A sealed package that arrives with its seal unbroken tells the receiver nobody changed what is inside. Data integrity asks the same of information. In the course: the concept of data integrity is to ensure that when data is sent from a source to a destination, the information received at the destination has not been altered in transit, Block Text p.56.

7.summary: Availability, the third goal of the CIA Triad, means the information is available when the user wants it; it is an often-overlooked part of information security.
7.deeper: Several solutions help maintain availability. Permissions limit who can delete data, so it is likely still there when needed. Regular backups of critical information let data that becomes corrupt or unavailable be restored. Fault tolerance (RAID) lets other drives provide the data if one hard drive fails. Clustering lets multiple servers act as one unit, so if one server fails another takes over the workload. Patching keeps a system up to date with service packs and security hot fixes, which reduces vulnerabilities and the chances of attack.
7.analogy: Availability is like a fire station that must answer whenever the call comes: spare trucks, spare crews and regular upkeep keep it ready, not just a lock on the door.
7.scenario: An Airman supports an e-mail service. To keep it available, the Airman clusters its servers so one can take over if another fails, uses RAID so a failed drive loses no data, and runs regular backups of critical information in case data becomes corrupt.
7.example: A shop that is locked and tidy still fails its customers if its doors never open when they come. Availability is the goal that information is there when wanted. In the course: availability is the concept of ensuring that the information is available when the user wants it, Block Text p.56.
